title: CT CASES/630223/2016 on 24 September, 2022
full_text: CT CASES/630223/2016 on 24 September, 2022 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 IN THE COURT OF MS. TWINKLE CHAWLA: MM, NI ACT-02, SOUTH- EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: NEW DELHI Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CIS number : DLSE020038832016 2. Name of the Complainant : Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. 3. Name of the Accused, : Smt. Sunita, R/o E-15, Ajmal Bagh, Noor parentage & residential Nagar Extn., Jamia Nagar, New Delhi address 4. Offence complained of or : U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act , proved 1881 5. Plea of the Accused : Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order : CONVICTED 7. Date of judgment/order : 24.09.2022 JUDGMENT 1. The Complainant has filed the present complaint under Section 138 / 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act ") against the Accused on the averments that Complainant had given a personal loan to the Accused under the personal loan agreement No. 0004/50/003/004180 for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/-; which was repayable in 60 installments of Rs. 3,648/- each. However, the Accused was irregular in payment of the EMIs and thereafter stopped paying the EMIs. The Page 1 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 Complainant then issued a loan recall notice to the Accused on 27.10.2015. 2. As per the Complainant, the Accused in discharge of her liability, issued a cheque bearing no. 511362 dated 13.11.2015 amounting to Rs. 1,85,582/- drawn on Indian Bank, Jamia Milia Islamia, Maulana Road, Ali Zauhar Road, Jamia Nagar, New Delhi-110025 (hereinafter referred as "cheque in question"). Upon presentation, the same was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 16.11.2015, for the reason "Funds Insufficient". The Complainant sent the legal demand notice dated 24.11.2015 through registered post at address of the Accused. Hence, despite the service of the legal demand notice, the Accused failed to make the payment within the stipulated period and the Complainant filed the present complaint. 3. As part of pre-summoning evidence, the AR of the Complainant Company tendered his pre-summoning evidence affidavit and also proved the following documents: Ex. CW1/A: Extract of resolution dated 11.09.2015, in favour of Sh. S. Alam. Ex. CW1/B: Copy of the Loan Agreement dated 13.01.2014 Ex. CW1/C: Statement of account from 13.0.2014 to 27.11.2015, qua the Accused. Ex. CW1/D: Certificate u/s 65B Indian Evidence Act, qua the statement of accounts. Ex. CW1/E: Original cheque bearing no. 511362 dated 13.11.2015 amounting to Rs. 1,85,582/- Ex. CW1/F: Original cheque returning memo dt. 16.11.2015. Ex. CW1/G: Legal Demand notice sent by the Complainant to the Accused, dated 24.11.2015. Ex. CW1/H: Postal receipt in respect of the legal Page 2 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 demand notice. Ex. CW1/I: Internet generated tracking report in respect of the legal demand notice. 4. After taking pre-summoning evidence, the Accused was ordered to be summoned in this case for commission of offence under Section 138 NI Act, vide order dated 07.01.2016. 5. Accused appeared and was released on bail on 09.06.2017. On finding a prima facie case, notice U/s 251 of the Criminal Procedure Code , 1973 (" CrPC ") was served upon the Accused on 09.06.2017 to which he pleaded not guilty and opted to contest after disclosing the following defence: "I do not plead guilty and claim trial. The impugned cheque bears my signature and was given towards the EMI to the complainant. The complainant used to deduct the EMI from my account as I was maintaining an account with complainant. I also gave some money personally. EMI was for Rs. 3300/-. I have already repaid 10 installments. The cheque in question has been misused by the complainant. I have no liability towards the complainant. I did not receive any legal notice." 6. Vide order dated 09.06.2017, opportunity was granted to the Accused to cross examine the Complainant. However, despite opportunity, the Accused did not cross- Page 3 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 examine the AR of the Complainant company, and hence, right to cross-examine the Complainant was closed by way of order dated 08.07.2019. 7. Thereafter, Accused was examined under Section 313 of CrPC on 26.10.2021 for explaining the circumstances appearing against her in the Complainant's evidence. She denied the Complainant's case and pleaded false implication in the present case and opted to lead evidence in her defence. The Accused examined herself as DW- 1 and brought on record her copy of share certificate issued by the Complainant and her salary slips, which is Ex. DW1/A and Ex. DW1/B (Colly) (OSR), respectively. 8. I have heard Ld. Counsel for the parties and have perused the case file along with the written submissions filed by the parties carefully and meticulously. Submissions of the Complainant and Accused 9. The Ld. Counsel for the Complainant has submitted that all ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are fulfilled in the present case and hence, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act arises in the favour of the Complainant, which has not been successfully rebutted by the Accused. 10.Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the Accused has submitted that the Accused deserves to be acquitted as the Accused has paid several EMIs and her liability is not of the cheque amount and that even the share certificates have not been adjusted against the liability. Hence, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act stands rebutted. Page 4 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 Legal Framework Ingredients of Section 138 NI Act: 11.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kusum Ingots & Alloys Ltd and Ors v. K Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd and Ors. , (2000) 2 SCC 745 ("Kusum Ingots Case"), has clearly stipulated that "the ingredients which are to be satisfied for making out a case under the provision are: (i) a person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge of any debt or other liability; 1 (ii) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (iii) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank; (iv) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the 1 Reduced to three months vide RBI circular dated 4.11.2011. Page 5 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 2 drawer of the cheque, within 15 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (v) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice; If the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied then the person who has drawn the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence." 12.Therefore, if the aforesaid ingredients are made out, the Accused is deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 NI Act. Presumption under Section 139 NI Act/ Section 118 NI Act: 13. Section 139 NI Act states that: "Presumption in favour of holder: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability" 14. Section 139 NI Act is a type of reverse onus clause, which stipulates a presumption in the favour of the Complainant as to fact of a cheque being received in discharge 2 The same is now enhanced to 30 days. Page 6 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 of a legal debt or liability. 15.Further, Section 118(a) of the NI Act, states as follows: "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. -- Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration --that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" 16.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has in a number of judgments dealt with the combined effect of the presumptions raised under Section 139 and Section 118(a) NI Act. 17.The following proposition can be summarized on a perusal of the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Sunil Todi & Ors v. State of Gujarat, LL 2021 SC 706 ("Sunil Todi Case"), Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian , 2021 SCC OnLine SC 75; APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Shakti International Fashion Linkers and Ors. , AIR 2020 SC 945; Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat and Ors., AIR 2019 SC 1876; Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513; K.N. Beena v. Muniyappan and Anr. , (2001) 8 SCC 458; and Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai v. State of Maharashtra , 1964 Cri. LJ 437: Page 7 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted; Section 139 of the NI Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability; (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the Accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities; (iii) Something which is probable has to be brought on record by the Accused for getting the burden of proof shifted to the Complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the Accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist; (iv) The words "unless the contrary is proved" which occur in Section 139 , make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by Section 139 NI Act cannot be said to be Page 8 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 rebutted; (v) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the Accused to rely on evidence led by him or the Accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the Complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely; (vi) That it is not necessary for the Accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Analysis 18.In the case at hand, it is not in dispute that the cheque in question was drawn by the Accused from her bank account and that she is the signatory of the cheque in question. Presentation of the cheque in question by the Complainant and its dishonour is also not in dispute. 19.The Complainant sent the legal demand notice, dated 24.11.2015 (Ex. CW1/G) by way of speed post (Ex. CW1/H). Though, it is the stand of the Accused that she has not received the legal demand notice; but it is noted that in her statement u/s 313 CrPC, she has stated that "the address mentioned on the legal demand notice is my correct address". Hence, the legal demand notice was sent on the correct address of Page 9 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 the Accused. Therefore, a presumption of due service is drawn u/s 27 of General Clauses Act, 1897; which provides that where the notice is sent by registered post to the correct address, the same shall be presumed to have been duly served. In M/s Darbar Exports and other v. Bank of India, 2003 (2) SCC (NI) 132 (Delhi), the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held that a presumption of service of notice is to be drawn where the notice is sent through registered post as well as UPC on correct address. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Hazi v. Palapetty Muhammad & Anr , (2007) 6SCC 555 has held that: "Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint U/s 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of complaint U/s 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required U/s 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary U/s 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act.". 20.Thus, the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/G is held to have been duly served upon the Accused. Finally, the complaint has been filed within the limitation period. Therefore, essential ingredients (i) to (v) as stipulated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kusum Ingots Case (supra), have been duly satisfied. Page 10 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 21. Further, as noted above, once the execution of the cheque by the Accused is proved/admitted, the presumption of the same being drawn for consideration stands attracted in terms of Section 139 NI Act. Now, in the case at hand, so far as the question of existence of basic ingredients for drawing of presumption U/s 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act is concerned, from the aforesaid discussion, it is apparent that the Accused has not denied her signatures on the cheque in question that has been drawn in favour of the Complainant on a bank account maintained by the Accused; and hence the said presumption can be drawn. The Ld. Counsel for the Accused has stated that such inference cannot be drawn as the cheque was issued as a blank signed cheque and the particulars on the same have been filled by or at the instance of the Complainant. At this stage, reliance can be laid on the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197; wherein it has been held that: "It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted... 38. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. This in itself would not invalidate the cheque. The onus would still be on the Accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or Page 11 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 liability by adducing evidence... 40. Even a blank cheque leaf voluntarily signed and handed over by the Accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt." (emphasis supplied) 22.The same view has been endorsed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Chopra v. State, CRL.M.C. 5211/2006. 23.Hence, in view of such clear stipulation by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and Hon'ble Delhi High Court, it is immaterial whether or not the particulars on the cheque have been filled by the Accused or not, to the extent the Accused has admitted to have appended her signatures on the cheque in question. Accordingly, the applicability of the presumption under Section 139 NI Act is not dependent upon the Accused filling the particulars on the cheque. Accordingly, it is required to be presumed that the cheque in question was drawn for consideration and the holder of the cheque i.e., the Complainant received the same in discharge of an existing debt. The onus, therefore, shifts on the Accused to establish a probable defence so as to rebut such a presumption. 24.In the segment on legal framework, set out above, the legal proposition with respect to the burden of proof upon the Accused has already been discussed. Hence, it is Page 12 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 now to be examined as to whether the Accused brought any material on record or pointed out glaring discrepancies in the material produced by the Complainant for dislodging the presumption which meets the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 25.The Accused in the present case, has taken the following line of defence with a view to rebut the presumption: (a) Cheque in question was issued a security cheque: 26.The Accused in her defence evidence as well as statement u/s 251 CrPC as well examination u/s 313 CrPC has submitted that the cheque in question was given as a security cheque and not for repayment, and hence, the provisions of Section 138 NI Act do not apply. In this regard, it is noted that the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Suresh Chandra Goyal v. Amit Singhal, Crl . L.P, 706/2014 has succinctly observed that: " Section 138 of NI Act does not distinguish between a cheque issued by the debtor in discharge of an existing debt or other liability, or a cheque issued as a security cheque on the premise that on the due future date the debt which shall have crystallized by then, shall be paid. So long as there is a debt existing, in respect whereof the cheque in question is issued, in my view, the same would attract Section 138 of NI Act in case of its dishonour." Page 13 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 27.Hence, it appears that if on the date of presentment of cheque, liability of the Accused existed towards the Complainant, the same would fall under Section 138 NI Act, even if the same was issued as a security cheque; and hence, it is not relevant if the cheque in question was issued with the intent of being a security cheque. In fact, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a recent judgment of the Sunil Todi Case (supra), has held that the provisions of Section 138 NI Act apply to cheques issued on advance basis as well, if at the time of presentation of the same, liability exists. It was observed that: "The object of the NI Act is to enhance the acceptability of cheques and inculcate faith in the efficiency of negotiable instruments for transaction of business. The purpose of the provision would become otiose if the provision is interpreted to exclude cases where debt is incurred after the drawing of the cheque but before its encashment. In Indus Airways, advance payments were made but since the purchase agreement was cancelled, there was no occasion of incurring any debt. The true purpose of Section 138 would not be fulfilled, if 'debt or other liability' is interpreted to include only a debt that exists as on the date of drawing of the cheque." (emphasis added) 28.Hence, unless it is shown that no liability existed on the date of presentation, either because loan had already been repaid by other modes or that no loan was taken; provision of Section 138 NI Act would apply to cheques issued on an advance basis Page 14 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 as well. Accordingly, this argument/defence of the Accused, by itself, does not rebut the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. (b) Liability of the Accused is less than the cheque amount: 29.The Accused has not denied the loan taken from the Complainant. In fact, in her examination u/s 313 CrPC, she has admitted the execution of Ex. CW1/B, i.e., the loan agreement with the Complainant. Hence, it is an admitted fact that an amount of Rs. 1,50,000/- was taken by the Accused, which was to be repaid in 60 EMIs of Rs. 3,648/-, on the terms and conditions set out in Ex. CW1/B. Further, the fact of default in payment of the EMIs is also not contested. 30.The only defence raised here is that the quantum of liability of the Accused is less than the cheque amount. It has been stated that the Accused has repaid Rs. 70,000 to Rs. 80,000/- to the Complainant. The Complainant has denied the receipt of the said amount. As per the statement of account, Ex. CW1/C, the Accused has only paid around Rs. 39,000/-; and that her loan account was turned NPA on 31.03.2015. The Accused, in support of her defence had produced salary slips, Ex. DW1/B (colly), wherein a monthly deduction was shown to be Rs. 8758/- for 8 months. While, in her examination in chief, the Accused stated that this payment was towards the present loan, in her cross-examination, she has conceded that she was acting as a guarantor in another loan advanced by the Complainant to one Ms. Nirmala Kumari and that the amount deducted in the salary slips, Ex. DW1/B Page 15 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 (colly) was regarding the loan of Ms. Nirmala Kumari. Accordingly, the said payment was admittedly not towards the present loan taken by her; but was the amount paid by her in her capacity as guarantor for the loan taken by Ms. Nirmala Kumari. 31.The other contention raised by the Accused is that her share certificates, which have also been issued by the Complainant, have not been deducted/adjusted in her liability. The said share certificates, which are Ex. DW1/A (Colly) are of the total value of Rs. 7500, as has been admitted by the Accused in her cross-examination dated 08.07.2022. No clause of the loan agreement or the share certificate has been pointed out by the Accused, wherein the said deduction was obligatory for the Complainant. 32. On the other hand, the Complainant has produced the loan agreement, Ex. CW1/B, a document executed between the parties with mutual consent, wherein it has been agreed that in addition to the interest of 16%, an additional interest of 2% per annum would lie on overdue installments. The default in payment of installments has been shown by the Complainant and not rebutted by the Accused. Accordingly, in terms of the loan agreement, the total outstanding from the Accused, as on 31.10.2015 was Rs. 1,88,734/-, which is more than the cheque amount. Further, while the loan was for 60 months, as per clause 3 of Ex. CW1/B, it was agreed between the parties that: Page 16 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 "if I fail to pay installments including interest as provided in clause 2 thereof, I shall be liable to pay at once the whole amount then due together with interest thereon in terms of my "DEMAND PROMISSORY NOTE" dated 13.01.14, if called upon to do so by the bank." 33.The AR of the Complainant has in his evidence affidavit stated that on 27.10.2015, a loan recall notice was sent to the Accused, to repay the entire amount due, due to her non-payment of EMIs. The AR of the Complainant, despite opportunity, has not been cross-examined by the Accused; thereby giving rise to an implicit admission of the issuance of this notice. Further, nowhere in the defence, has it been stated that the loan recall notice was not issued. Accordingly, in terms of the loan agreement, in the event of default of payment of EMIs, (which has occurred in the present case), the Complainant was at liberty to demand payment of the complete amount due, even prior to expiry of the duration of the loan. Even a demand promissory note has been executed by the Accused for the total amount alongwith interest. Hence, the Complainant has demonstrated the basis of liability of the Accused. However, the defence of the Accused that her liability is less than the cheque amount, has not been proved by the Accused by the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 34.In these circumstances and in view of the above detailed discussion, this court is of the considered opinion that the Accused has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in favour of the Complainant and ingredients of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 are fully proved. Page 17 of 18 Jamia Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Sunita CC No. 630223/2016 35.Therefore, Accused is held guilty and convicted for commission of offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881. Let her be heard on the quantum of sentence on 12.10.2022 at 12:00 noon. ORDER: CONVICTED Announced in Open Court (Twinkle Chawla) MM (NI-Act 02), South East Saket Court, New Delhi Note: This judgment contains 18 pages and each page has been signed by me.
